title: The New Year's Eve 1944 concert flyer with Parker at the bottom
summary: The advertisement hyped Dizzy, Dexter, Sarah and Blakey but listed Charlie Parker last, showing how little he was known.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Around that time, 1945, after playing the Apollo Theatre, we started our trek South again. We played the Apollo Theatre that Christmas, I believe, or during Christmas week or the holiday week, and after that we started to trek South in early 1945.

I do remember on New Year's Eve, just before 1945, they had a session, I guess, a Jazz concert, at a place called Manhattan Square. I've forgotten who it was that produced this thing, but it was Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker, it was Art Blakey, Dexter Gordon and Gene Ammons, and Tommy Potter, myself, Don Byas, and a couple of other people I can't remember. But I still have this waiver that they had that advertised is. I still have it at home.

The funny part about it was, they had all sorts of accolades that they paid tribute to different artists. I remember at the top of it, they advertised this thing as "Dizzy Gillespie, The Wizard of the Trumpet. Dexter Gordon, A Weird Tenor Man. Gene Ammons Blows Like Mad. Sarah Vaughan

(they spelled 'Sarah' 'S-a-r-a), Beautiful New Vocalist. Art Blakey, Drummer, Kicks Like Mad." They had my name spelled "M-a-l-e-c-h-i" and then they had "Johnny" -- "Johnny Malachi, Brilliant Young Pianist and Arranger." And they had "Tommy Potter, bass." And Don Byas, they had something to say about him There were some other people on it... They even had Baby Laurence, the dancer, they had him on there. Because Baby Laurence used to make sessions with the musicians. It was just like another instrument. I think he's the greatest tap dancer I've ever seen. But right down at the bottom of the page, they have written "Charley Parker, Alto Sax" -- down at the bottom of the page.

A lot of people ask me, especially students at the school and everything, about Charlie Parker. They think back during those days of him being.... Well, they know of him now as a legend, but they don't realize that back then few people knew him or liked what he was doing, anything. And these were these smart people in New York who were producing these concerts and things, where he is the one that should have been at the top of the page!

I have this particular thing... It's recorded down at the Smithsonian Institute, they take a picture of it. And I keep it just for that particular reason, because I think it's somewhat of a collector's thing, or a very historic thing, to
realize that this guy who dominated the Jazz world at one time was just somebody that nobody knew or respected in any sense.
So that was on New Year's Eve of 1944.
